traditions.d: Kyoto silk weaving for the court and aristocracy, today chiefly luxury obi and kimono cloth.
traditions.tech: Brocade, damask, tsumugi, kasuri and velvet weaving; Jacquard looms adopted in the Meiji era
traditions.mat: Raw and scoured silk, gold thread and gilded paper
traditions.auth: Woven-in three-dimensional patterning and metallic threads; top obi can reach about 1 million yen.

traditions.d: Kyoto paste-resist dyeing of pictorial designs on kimono silk, credited to fan painter Miyazaki Yūzensai.
traditions.tech: Hand-painting within itome-nori rice-paste outlines; stencil (kata) yūzen from the Meiji era; gold leaf and embroidery finishing
traditions.mat: Silk, rice-paste resist, gojiru soybean base, dyes, gold and platinum leaf
traditions.auth: Fine white or coloured outlines left by the paste, brushwork gradations and metallic finishing; hand-painted (itome) work versus stencil imitation.

traditions.d: Kanazawa yūzen dyeing with lifelike natural scenes in gentle gradients, more naturalistic than Kyō-yūzen.
traditions.tech: Paste-resist yūzen dyeing with realistic motifs such as insect-nibbled leaves
traditions.auth: Realistic flora with worm-eaten leaf details and soft shading rather than Kyoto's framed, gilded pictures.

traditions.mat: Silk, Techigi bark, iron-rich mud, igisu seaweed paste
traditions.auth: 'Honba Amami-Oshima Tsumugi' certificate at the foot of the bolt; Amami union globe seal or Kagoshima union two-flag seal.

notes: Old 'Sash' (k112) became Obi (Japanese kimono sash; old s replaced by the Obi Wikipedia page). Hakama SKU flood (26 Tozando/SeidoShop/Mitsuboshi SKUs) cut to four maker-level versions under the Umanori archetype; old type names became archetypes. Kimono 'Hitoe' became a t type (unlined). Old Ruqun models Qixiong/Qiyao became archetypes; old Beizi chang/duan became t types. New kinds Qipao, Mamianqun, Zhongshan suit, Tang jacket sourced from Wikipedia. Left out (no page retrieved or facts unconfirmed): Y. & Sons, Kyoto Kimono Yuzen, Hanbok Lynn (no retrievable page); Longqingxiang (no source); Tatsumura Textile has no register entry (named only in Nishijin-ori tradition). Ruifuxiang founding: Wikipedia gives 1862 (Jinan), gov.cn gives 1893 (Meng Luochuan) for the Beijing house; register uses 1862. Dior referenced by register name 'Dior' (entry assumed from another shelf).
